narrative:
The model estimates you have a 17% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a high probability, it is enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction that you are at risk of failing is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this actually pushes the model toward predicting you will fail. Among students who passed, having zero previous failures is the norm, but in your specific combination of circumstances the model sees the complete lack of any prior academic struggle as a warning sign rather than a strength. 

The second strongest influence is your strong desire to pursue higher education, which works in your favor and pulls the prediction toward passing. The third key factor is your mother’s job as a teacher. This also pulls the prediction toward passing, yet not strongly enough to overcome the first factor.

Because the absence of any past failures weighed most heavily against you, the school wants you to use the remedial courses to build consistent study habits now, before any problems appear. You should treat this requirement as an early opportunity: focus on increasing your weekly study time beyond the two hours you currently spend, since most successful students study 2–5 hours. Building that routine while you still have no failures can turn the 17% risk into a much safer outlook.
